questions.stem: What is the operation of adding a new element at the rear of a queue called?
questions.explanation: Insertion at the rear end of a queue is called enqueue, and removal from the front is called dequeue. Push belongs to a stack, and peek merely looks at the front element without removing it.

optionRationale.1: Dequeue removes an element from the front of the queue.
optionRationale.3: Push is the insertion operation of a stack, not of a queue.
optionRationale.4: Peek only reads the front element without changing the queue.

questions.objective: Name the insertion operation of a queue

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a typical use of a queue?
options: Going back to the previous page in a web browser
Waiting list for a railway reservation
Customers waiting at a bank counter
questions.explanation: The back button of a browser returns to the page visited most recently, which is last in first out and so is a stack application. Printer jobs, railway waiting lists and bank counters serve the earliest arrival first and are queues.

optionRationale.2: People are served in the order in which they joined, which is a queue.
optionRationale.3: Print jobs are processed in order of submission, which is a queue.
optionRationale.4: Customers are served first come first served, which is a queue.

questions.objective: Separate queue uses from stack uses

questions.stem:
What is printed by this code?
`q = [1, 2, 3]`
`q.append(4)`
`print(q[0])`
questions.explanation: append() adds 4 at the rear, so q becomes [1, 2, 3, 4]. The front of a list-based queue is index 0, which holds 1, the element that joined first, and this is what q[0] prints.

optionRationale.1: 4 is the element that has just joined at the rear; q[0] is the front element.
optionRationale.3: 3 was the rear before append(); q[0] is the front, the oldest element.
optionRationale.4: print(q[0]) shows a single element, not the whole list.

questions.objective: Locate the front of a list-based queue

questions.stem:
What is printed by this code?
`q = [1, 2, 3, 4]`
`for _ in range(3):`
`    q.append(q.pop(0))`
`print(q)`
questions.explanation: Each pass removes the front element and adds it at the rear, so the list rotates left by one place: [2, 3, 4, 1], then [3, 4, 1, 2], and after the third pass [4, 1, 2, 3].

optionRationale.1: This is the list after only one rotation; the loop runs three times.
optionRationale.2: This is the list after two rotations; one more rotation is needed.
optionRationale.3: This would need four rotations, which brings the list back to its start.

questions.stem:
In the code below a letter is added to the queue and the letter "x" removes one element from the front. What is printed?
`q = []`
`rem = []`
`for ch in "ABxCxxD":`
`    if ch == "x":`
`        rem.append(q.pop(0))`
`    else:`
`        q.append(ch)`
`print(q, rem)`
questions.explanation: A and B join: [A, B]. The first x removes A, leaving [B]. C joins: [B, C]. The next x removes B and the next x removes C, leaving an empty queue. D then joins. So q is [D] and the removed letters, in order, are A, B and C.

optionRationale.2: Removal is always from the front, so the first removed letter is A, the earliest to join, then B.
optionRationale.3: There are three x characters, so three elements are removed, including C.
optionRationale.4: pop(0) takes the oldest element each time; the removed items are A, B and C in that order.

questions.objective: Trace enqueue and dequeue driven by a string

questions.stem: Match each term of a queue in List-I with its meaning in List-II.
questions.explanation: Elements are removed at the front (I) and added at the rear (II). Overflow occurs when an element is added to a queue that has no space left (III), and underflow occurs when an element is removed from a queue that has none (IV).

optionRationale.1: Elements leave at the front and join at the rear; A and B are exchanged here.
optionRationale.2: Overflow is a full queue and underflow is an empty queue; C and D are exchanged here.
optionRationale.4: Front and rear are the two ends of the queue; overflow and underflow are error conditions, not ends.

right: I. End from which elements are removed
II. End at which elements are added
III. Trying to add to a queue that is full
IV. Trying to remove from a queue that is empty

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about queues and deques.
A. A queue is a linear data structure.
B. In a queue deletion is done at the rear.
C. Underflow occurs when a dequeue is attempted on an empty queue.
D. A deque can be used to behave like a stack.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A queue keeps its elements in a line, so it is linear (A is true). Deletion is from the front, so B is false. Dequeue on an empty queue is underflow (C is true). A deque with insertion and deletion at one same end behaves as a stack (D is true).

optionRationale.1: B is false: deletion takes place at the front, not the rear; C is also correct.
optionRationale.2: B is false because the rear is the end at which insertion is done.
optionRationale.4: B is false (deletion is at the front), and C is a correct statement.

questions.objective: Judge statements about queues and deques

questions.stem:
A deque is stored in a list with index 0 as the front. What does this code print?
`d = []`
`for i in range(1, 6):`
`    if i % 2:`
`        d.append(i)`
`    else:`
`        d.insert(0, i)`
`d.pop(0)`
`d.pop()`
`print(d)`
questions.explanation: Odd numbers join at the rear and even numbers at the front. The list grows as [1], [2, 1], [2, 1, 3], [4, 2, 1, 3], [4, 2, 1, 3, 5]. pop(0) then removes the front 4 and pop() removes the rear 5, leaving [2, 1, 3].

optionRationale.2: The last pop() removes the rear element 5 and pop(0) removes 4, so 3 stays as the last item, not 4 at the front.
optionRationale.3: Two elements are removed, one from each end, so only three remain.
optionRationale.4: The front element 4 is removed by pop(0), and 5 by pop(); four elements cannot remain.

questions.objective: Trace a deque with insertions at both ends

questions.stem:
What does this code print?
`q = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`
`while len(q) > 1:`
`    q.append(q.pop(0))`
`    q.pop(0)`
`print(q[0])`
questions.explanation: Each pass moves the front element to the rear and then deletes the new front. Starting from [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]: [3, 4, 5, 1], then [5, 1, 3], then [3, 5]; the last pass moves 3 to the rear giving [5, 3] and deletes 5. Only 3 is left.

optionRationale.1: 1 is moved to the rear in the first pass and removed in the third pass, so it does not survive.
optionRationale.2: 5 is moved to the rear in the third pass and is deleted in the last pass, so it does not survive.
optionRationale.3: 2 is removed in the very first pass, right after 1 has been moved to the rear.

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): In a list-based deque with index 0 as the front, starting from an empty list, the statements `insert(0, 5)` and `append(7)` followed by `pop(0)` make pop(0) return 5.
Reason (R): insert(0, item) places the item before all other elements, so the item inserted last at the front stays at the front until it is removed.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: insert(0, 5) puts 5 at the front and append(7) adds 7 at the rear. The front element is 5, so pop(0) returns 5 and the assertion is true. The reason states exactly why: insert at index 0 sits before every other element, so it is the first one removed from the front.

optionRationale.2: The reason is the cause of the result, so it explains the assertion.
optionRationale.3: The reason is true: insert(0, item) puts the item in front of all others.
optionRationale.4: The assertion is true: pop(0) takes the front element, which is 5.

questions.objective: Reason about insertion and deletion at the front of a deque
